title: Food and nutrition
content_markdown:
The food we eat impacts our physical, mental, social, and spiritual wellbeing\. Our eating habits reflect our identities, traditions, values, and life circumstances\. Knowing the factors that influence food choices is key to building a healthy and meaningful relationship with food\.

Many students face challenges in accessing food and maintaining a balanced diet, such as financial barriers, limited time and energy, lack of food skills, or difficulty finding familiar and culturally relevant food\. This issue is also affected by larger social and political systems\. At UBC, a range of food and nutrition resources are available to help you navigate these challenges, including, but not limited to, accessing affordable groceries, expanding your food skills and knowledge by learning how to prepare simple and nutritious meals, or finding support for food and nutrition\-related concerns\.

## Nutrition[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/wellness\-resources/food\-nutrition/\#nutrition](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/food-nutrition/#nutrition)

**

How can I eat well?

**

Eating well looks different for everyone\. Generally, it begins with developing basic food skills, such as planning and budgeting  for meals, grocery shopping, reading food labels, and preparing simple dishes\. You should aim to have a variety of nutrient\-dense foods throughout the day, such as vegetables and fruits, whole grains, and plant\-based proteins, while making water your main drink of choice\.

There is no single “best” way to eat healthily\. While [Canada’s Food Guide](https://food-guide.canada.ca/en/food-guide-snapshot/) can be a helpful resource, it’s essential to recognize its limitations, particularly in addressing social and cultural dimensions of food and the harm it has historically caused, including its role in the mistreatment of Indigenous peoples\. Sharing and enjoying culturally meaningful foods is an important way to nourish your body, honour tradition, and build a positive relationship with food\.

**

I have specific dietary needs\. Where can I get help?

**

Everyone’s food choices can look different depending on their specific dietary needs\. Whether it’s [celiac disease](https://food.ubc.ca/category/celiac-disease-and-gluten-free/), plant\-based eating, [food allergies](https://food.ubc.ca/nutrition/allergies/), or religious dietary needs, there are resources to support you\.

Below are a few example resources available to UBC students:

-   If you are a varsity athlete, read [athlete nutrition guides](https://gothunderbirds.ca/sports/2016/7/5/nutrition.aspx) developed by the sport dietitian at UBC Athlete Nutrition\.
-   For students looking for Halal foods, the UBC Muslim Student Association created a [Halal Food Guide](https://msaubc.org/halal-food-guide-2024) \(pdf\)\.
-   If you live in residence, connect with the [dietitian in Residence](https://food.ubc.ca/contact-the-dietitian/)\.

**

How can I connect with a dietitian?

**

Dietitians are trained professionals who can help you find strategies to eat well according to your unique dietary needs\. You can speak to a dietitian in person, online, or over the phone\.

-   **UBC Residence Dietitian**  
    If you are a student living in residence, contact the [dietitian in residence](https://www.food.ubc.ca/contact-the-dietitian/) to discuss a food allergy, intolerance, nutrition\-related medical condition, or other concerns\.
-   **Dietitian Services at HealthLink BC**  
    If you are a British Columbia resident, you can call 811 \(or 711 for the hearing impaired\) to speak with a registered dietitian free of charge\. They are available by phone Monday to Friday from 9:00 am to 5:00 pm PT\. You do not need a referral from your healthcare provider\. You can also find information on [various food and nutrition](https://www.healthlinkbc.ca/healthy-eating-physical-activity) topics on the HealthLink BC website\.
-   **Find a dietitian in British Columbia**  
    [BC dietitians](https://www.bcdietitians.ca/) provides an online directory of registered dietitians in BC by location and specialty areas\. You can also search for dietitians across Canada through the [Dietitians of Canada](https://members.dietitians.ca/Web/Web/Membership/Directory/Member-Directory.aspx) directory\.
-   **AMS/GSS Student Health Plan**  
    All UBC students under the [AMS/GSS Student Health Plan](https://www.ams.ubc.ca/support-services/health-dental/) can submit claims of $20 per visit to see a dietitian, to a maximum of $400 per policy year\. You will need a physician referral to qualify for this health benefit\. Some dietitians might have student rates or a sliding scale for their services\.

**

I want to learn more about food, nutrition, and explore my relationship with food and body\. Where do I start?

**

There are available resources to support you in learning more about food and nutrition and reflecting on your personal relationship with food and body\. Throughout the Winter Session, you can also find a variety of workshops and events focusing on building food and nutrition knowledge and skills offered by the Food Hub Market and UBC Food Services\.

Below are some example resources provided by UBC and other organizations in Canada:

-   [UBC Food Services Nutrition Resource Hub](https://food.ubc.ca/nutrition/)
-   [UnlockFood\.ca](https://www.unlockfood.ca/en/default.aspx)
-   [Healthy Eating On Campus](https://food-guide.canada.ca/en/tips-for-healthy-eating/healthy-eating-campus/)
-   [Body image, disordered eating, and eating disorders](https://foundrybc.ca/resource/body-image-disordered-eating-eating-disorders/)
-   [National Eating Disorder Information Centre](https://nedic.ca/)
-   [https://amscampusbase\.ubc\.ca/club\_signup?category\_tags\=4794335&group\_type\=40186](https://amscampusbase.ubc.ca/club_signup?category_tags=4794335&group_type=40186)[Food Hub Market](https://www.instagram.com/ubcfoodhubmarket/?hl=en)
-   [UBC Food Services](https://www.instagram.com/ubcfoodie/?hl=en)

## Food security[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/wellness\-resources/food\-nutrition/\#food\-security](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/food-nutrition/#food-security)

**

How do I eat well on a budget?

**

Browse money\-saving strategies to help your food budget last\. Below are some ways to get started:

-   **Prepare your own meals**  
    Preparing food at home is an effective way to save food dollars\. Try batch cooking or packing leftovers for lunch\. You can find simple recipes on [UBC Food Services](https://food.ubc.ca/category/easy-recipes/) or [Food Guide Kitchen](https://food-guide.canada.ca/en/kitchen/) websites\.
-   **Plan ahead**  
    Knowing [how to plan your meals](https://www.unlockfood.ca/en/Articles/Budget/10-Tips-for-Planning-Meals-on-a-Budget.aspx) and having [practical ways to save money](https://www.unlockfood.ca/en/Articles/Budget/20-Ways-to-Save-Money-on-Your-Groceries.aspx) before grocery shopping can help you maximize your budget\. Consider buying in bulk with a friend or roommate  to save on grocery costs\. You can also try using apps, such as [Flipp](https://flipp.com/), [Flashfood](https://www.flashfood.com/#How-it-works), [Checkout 51](https://www.checkout51.com/), and [Too Good to Go](https://toogoodtogo.ca/en-ca/) to find food and grocery deals\.
-   **Check out UBC’s low\-cost food initiatives**  
    The [UBC Food Hub](https://foodhub.ubc.ca/) continues to work hard to share both student\-led and university\-led, low\-cost food resources and food security initiatives, such as the [Food Hub Market](https://foodhub.ubc.ca/market/)\. 
-   **Support student\-led food initiatives** ​​​​​  
    From September to April, visit student\-run cafes like [Agora Café](https://blogs.ubc.ca/agora/) and [UBC Sprouts](http://www.ubcsprouts.ca/) for low\-cost nutritious options\. Sprouts hosts initiatives like [Community Eats](http://www.ubcsprouts.ca/community-eats), and faculties and student groups organize food\-related community events\.

**

What if I don’t have enough money for food?

**

Food insecurity disproportionately affects international students, graduate students, disabled students, queer and trans communities, as well as individuals who identify as Indigenous, Black, or Persons of Colour\. Below are some places to get started if you find yourself making difficult choices around food due to financial barriers\.

-   Connect with your [Enrolment Services Advisor](https://students.ubc.ca/about-student-services/enrolment-services-advisors/) \(ESA\)\. If you don’t have enough money for food, your ESA can help you with budgeting, access to emergency funds, or other types of financial assistance\.
-   Emergency food relief is available on campus through the [AMS Food Bank](https://www.ams.ubc.ca/support-services/student-services/food-bank/), [Acadia Food Hub](http://acadiafoodhub.ca/), and student\-led initiatives such as [Sprouts Free Meals initiative](http://www.ubcsprouts.ca/free-meal-program) and the [community fridge](http://www.ubcsprouts.ca/community-fridge)\. You can also find free or low\-cost food resources in the community through [Vancouver Neighbourhood Food Networks](https://vancouverfoodnetworks.com/#networks), [Vancouver Coastal Health food asset maps](https://www.vch.ca/en/service/food-asset-maps), and [Fraser Health’s free and low\-cost food directory](https://www.fraserhealth.ca/health-topics-a-to-z/free-and-low-cost-food-directory)\.

Learn more about food security as well as food and financial resources through the [Food Hub](https://foodhub.ubc.ca/)\.

## Cooking and meal planning[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/wellness\-resources/food\-nutrition/\#cooking\-and\-meal\-planning](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/food-nutrition/#cooking-and-meal-planning)

**

I’m new to cooking on my own\. Where do I start?

**

Cooking on your own for the first time can be intimidating\. Here are some ways you can get started\. 

-   **Go on a free virtual grocery store tour**  
    Join UBC nutrition students on a [virtual grocery store tour](http://food.ubc.ca/virtual_store_tours/) as they guide you through navigating a grocery store, reading labels, and choosing foods that fit into your budget\.
-   **Learn from others**  
    Attend a food\-based workshop on campus with different [student clubs](https://www.ams.ubc.ca/student-life/clubs/) and UBC groups, like the UBC Cooking Club\. The [Food Hub market](https://www.instagram.com/ubcfoodhubmarket/?hl=en) hosts events where students can learn to make simple and healthy recipes from scratch while simultaneously expanding their food knowledge and skillset\. They also post videos and recipes for easy and nutritious meals and snacks\.
-   **Practice, practice, practice**  
    Check out tips from UBC Food Services on [learning how to cook](https://food.ubc.ca/category/learn-to-cook/) and read these 5 tips from a fellow student on [cooking as a beginner](https://students.ubc.ca/ubclife/5-honest-thoughts-about-cooking-beginner)\. 

**

How can I save time on meal planning and preparation?

**

Life as a student is busy\. Balancing academics along with other responsibilities and aspects of student life can make it hard to find time to put together a nourishing meal\. Below are some tips you can try:

-   **Have an ongoing grocery list**  
    A running list on your fridge or phone can help you keep track of the items you need when going to the grocery store\. You can categorize these based on where you find the items in the store \(e\.g\., bakery, fruits\) to save time and reduce impulsive purchases\.
-   **Stock up on kitchen staples**  
    Find which ingredients are [staples in your diet](https://food.ubc.ca/15-convenient-kitchen-pantry-staples/) and keep them available for when you need to quickly put a meal together\. 
-   **Order groceries online**  
    If you don’t have time, order ahead and pick up your groceries in stores\. Many grocery stores offer this service for a small fee\.
-   **Meal prep or batch cook with a friend**  
    Check out [11 meal prep ideas](https://food.ubc.ca/11-ideas-for-meal-prep-day/) for tasks you can do ahead of time\. Double the portions when you make a meal\. Invite your friends and have each person take on a different task at the same time to speed up the process\.

title: Sexual health
content_markdown:
For many people, sex, sexual health, and sexuality are an important part of wellbeing throughout the various stages of life and development\. Sexual activity and sexual health influence our physical and emotional wellbeing, as well as our relationships with others\. 

Learning more about sex, relationships, and sexual health can help you have experiences that are thoughtful, respectful, informed, and enjoyable\.

## Enjoying and exploring sex[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/sexual\-health/\#enjoying\-and\-exploring\-sex](https://students.ubc.ca/health/sexual-health/#enjoying-and-exploring-sex)

### Get to know your body

One of the best ways to learn about your sexuality and what feels good for you is by getting to know your own body and preferences\. Many people did not grow up in a culture that supports open and honest conversations about pleasure or sex\. Sexual health education in school can also differ greatly from one community to the next\. Continuing to learn and ask questions about these topics can be a rewarding and healthy part of our sexuality and our sexual experiences\.

Exploring which sensations your body likes and responds to—through self\-pleasure or masturbation—can help you understand what feels good and safe for you, either on your own, with a partner, or with a sex tool or toy\.

The UBC [Wellness Centre Sexual Health Shop](https://students.ubc.ca/health/sexual-health/wellness-centre-sexual-health-shop/) sells a variety of sex toys, lubricants, masturbation aids, and safety supplies that are geared towards a variety of bodies and sensations\. They also have trained peer educators on\-site available to speak confidentially about any questions you may have, or products you’d like to try\.

### Engaging in sexual activity is entirely up to you

If you are thinking about masturbating, or engaging in sexual activity, there is a lot to think about\. This is a personal decision that should empower you to think and talk about what might feel best for you—honest, consensual conversations are the first step\. There are a lot of conflicting messages coming from the media, stigmatized voices, cultural forces, pornography, and even from our peers\.

Check in with your thoughts, feelings, and the physical sensations in your body\. Consider the following reflection questions:

-   How do I know if and when I’m ready for sex? \(for the first time or for the 100th time\)
-   How do I know what sexual activities or sensations I am comfortable with?
-   How do I know what my boundaries are and how can I assert them?

Ensuring that you slow down to think, research, and talk to trusted sources will set you up for a pleasurable and rewarding experience—if and when you feel ready\. The choice to engage in sexual activity is personal, and everyone has the right to make that choice for themselves\.

### Consent is key

Consent is necessary and required for any type of sexual activity\. This includes, but is not limited to kissing, making out, touching, sexting, sharing sexy photos, and all other forms of sexual activity\. 

When we use the word *sex*, this refers to all types of sexual interactions, not just penetrative intercourse\. It refers to the full range of sexual acts and experiences, all of which require consent\. In fact, it’s the law\! Read more about the [Canadian legal implications of consent](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/erase/school-and-online-safety/consent)\.

Above all, sexual consent requires clear communication, as well as attentive listening and attention to signals and body language\. Research tells us that setting boundaries around what’s okay and what’s not okay for you sexually can lead to better, more enjoyable sexual experiences\. It’s important to clearly communicate your boundaries and ask for what you need, as well as to look and listen for your partner’s signals and directives\.

Learn more about [consent](https://svpro.ubc.ca/education/consent/) and how to make sure everyone involved feels informed, comfortable, and respected\.

## Exploring safe or safer sex[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/sexual\-health/\#exploring\-safe\-or\-safer\-sex](https://students.ubc.ca/health/sexual-health/#exploring-safe-or-safer-sex)

Feeling safe, informed, and prepared for sexual encounters can make sex more fun, respectful, and comfortable\. Safe sex is all about caring for yourself and your partner\(s\), and safety is part of the responsibility and maturity of being ready for a sexual relationship\.

This section covers ways to protect your health, including how to prevent STIs, use birth control, and find support and information around pregnancy\.

### Sexually Transmitted Infections \(STIs\)

STIs, short for [Sexually Transmitted Infections](https://www.sexandu.ca/stis/) and also known as STBBIs, [Sexual Transmitted and Blood Borne Infections](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/infectious-diseases/sexual-health-sexually-transmitted-infections/canadian-guidelines/stbbi-prevention-guide.html), are infections most commonly passed through fluid exchange or skin\-to\-skin contact during sex\.

While people may not always show signs or symptoms of having an STI, the infections, if left untreated, can develop into serious health concerns and be unknowingly passed onto others\. STIs and blood borne viruses can affect anybody who has any type of sex\.

They are many different types of Sexually Transmitted Infections \(STIs\), and they can be:

-   **Bacterial**, such as [Chlamydia](https://shvic.org.au/stis-and-bbvs/chlamydia),  [Gonborrhea](https://hi.easternhealth.ca/healthy-living/sexual-health/stis/gonorrhea/), [Syphilis](https://hi.easternhealth.ca/healthy-living/sexual-health/stis/syphilis/), and [Mycoplasma Genitalium \(Mgen\)](https://shvic.org.au/stis-and-bbvs/mycoplasma-genitalium)
-   **Viral**, including HPV \(Human Papillomavirus\), [Hepatitis](https://shvic.org.au/stis-and-bbvs/hepatitis-a-b-and-c), [HIV \(Human Immunodeficiency Virus\)](https://hi.easternhealth.ca/healthy-living/sexual-health/stis/human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv/), [Mpox \(MonkeyPox\)](https://shvic.org.au/stis-and-bbvs/monkeypox), and [Genital Herpes \(HSV\)](https://shvic.org.au/stis-and-bbvs/genital-herpes)
-   **Parasitic**, like [Pubic lice](https://shvic.org.au/stis-and-bbvs/pubic-lice-scabies), Trichomoniasis, or Scabies

There are also **Fungal infections** that are not STIs, but can spread through sexual contact, such as [yeast infections \(gential thrush\)](https://shvic.org.au/for-you/genital-health/genital-thrush)\.

Anyone who is or who has been sexually active is at risk for Sexually Transmitted Infections \(STIs\)\. However, STIs can be prevented through awareness and proper protection and prevention measures\. If contracted, many STIs are treatable or manageable, and many are curable\.

#### Preventing the Transmission of STIs

STIs can be transmitted through vaginal sex, anal sex, and oral sex, as well as other types of skin\-to\-skin contact\. They can also be passed on by touching the genitals with fingers \(if you have infected fluids on your hands\) or the sharing of sex toys\. 

Below are some ways to stay safe and to prevent the transmission of STIs\.

**

Talk openly about safe or safer sex

**

Talking openly with your sexual partner\(s\) about things like STI prevention, testing history, preventative methods, preferred products, and any possible symptoms or infections can help keep everyone safe\. It also helps build trust and shows respect for each other, which is part of every healthy sexual relationship\.

**

Use protection

**

Consider using a barrier method of STI prevention for vaginal, anal, or oral sex\. Barrier methods are designed to restrict infected cells passing from one body to another\. They also keep sperm from reaching an egg\.

Types of barriers include condoms \(internal and external\), oral dams, diaphragms, cervical caps, and the contraceptive sponge\. Not all barrier methods of contraception protect against STIs—only condoms and oral dams provide STI prevention\. Oral dams can provide STI protection for oral sex, as well as genital and anal stimulation\. Many people use one or more types of protection during sex, especially if they are looking to prevent a pregnancy, as well as STIs\.

Free internal and external condoms are available at the [Wellness Centre](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/wellness-centre/), [SVPRO](https://svpro.ubc.ca/), and [AMS SASC](https://www.amssasc.ca/)\. You can also buy specialized condoms and oral dams from the [Wellness Centre Sexual Health Shop](https://students.ubc.ca/health/sexual-health/wellness-centre-sexual-health-shop/)\.

Condoms are also available for purchase at any drug store or pharmacy\. There are different types of products for different bodies; some are made of latex, and some aren’t\. People usually try a few different products before learning what is right for them\.Staff at the [Wellness Centre Sexual Health Shop](https://students.ubc.ca/health/sexual-health/wellness-centre-sexual-health-shop/) can also provide more information about safer sex practices and answer any questions about sexual health\.

**

Get vaccinated

**

Getting the [HPV and Hepatitis A and B vaccines](https://smartsexresource.com/sexually-transmitted-infections/sti-basics/preventing-stis/#vaccines) helps provide protection against STIs\. Check your vaccination history and talk to a healthcare provider or a pharmacist to keep your vaccinations up\-to\-date if possible\. You can also get vaccinated at [Student Health and Wellbeing](https://students.ubc.ca/health/medical-care-on-campus/) on campus\. There may be a cost for certain vaccines, while some are covered through your extended health plan\.

**

Get tested

**

Many STIs have no symptoms\. Getting an STI test is the only way to know if you or a sexual partner has any STIs\.

Most testing options are fast, confidential, and painless\. When you are getting tested, this is a good opportunity to ask your healthcare provider what the test includes, and any further information on protection, prevention, and risk factors\. 

If you test positive, your provider will recommend treatment and connect you with additional support and resources\. Many STIs are manageable or even curable, if they are tested for and diagnosed early\. If STIs go untreated, they can lead to more complicated and serious illnesses\.

For STI testing on campus, visit [Student Health and Wellbeing](https://students.ubc.ca/health/medical-care-on-campus/)\. For clinics outside of campus, use the [Smart Sex Clinic Finder tool](https://smartsexresource.com/get-tested/what-to-expect)\.

**

Use PrEP, PEP, or Doxy\-PEP

**

**PrEP**, short for [Pre\-Exposure Prophylaxis](https://shvic.org.au/for-you/prep-pre-exposure-prophylaxis), is a tablet that reduces the risk of being infected with HIV and can be taken by people who are HIV\-negative\. If someone is exposed to HIV, the medication in PrEP stops HIV from multiplying and establishing itself in the body\. PrEP prevents HIV, but does not prevent any other STIs\. People of all genders, sexualities and bodies may be eligible for PrEP\.

**PEP**, short for [Post\-Exposure Prophylaxis](https://smartsexresource.com/topics/post-exposure-prophylaxis-pep), is a medication that can prevent HIV infection after a possible exposure\. It must be started within 3 days after the potential HIV exposure, but the sooner it’s taken, the more effective it is\.

**Doxy\-PEP**, short for [Doxycycline  Post\-Exposure Prophylaxis](https://shvic.org.au/for-you/doxy-pep-doxycycline-post-exposure-prophylaxis), is an oral dose of an antibiotic called doxycycline that is taken within 72 hours \(3 days\) of having sex \(oral, anal, or vaginal\) to protect against syphilis and chlamydia\. Doxy\-PEP is most likely to benefit people at higher risk of syphilis, such as gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men \(GBMSM\), and transgender women, especially with recent syphilis or multiple recent STIs\. Doxy\-PEP is not 100% effective for all STIs\. Regular STI testing is still recommended when taking it\.

## Pregnancy and birth control[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/sexual\-health/\#pregnancy\-and\-birth\-control](https://students.ubc.ca/health/sexual-health/#pregnancy-and-birth-control)

### Pregnancy

If you know or think you may be pregnant, taking a pregnancy test is a good first step\. There are many options for tests and many are available at any drug store or pharmacy in British Columbia\. There are also low\-cost pregnancy test options for purchase at the [Wellness Centre](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/wellness-centre/) on campus\. If a pregnancy test is confirmed as positive, the next best step is to talk to a medical professional\.

A doctor or nurse can also do a pregnancy test for you, and discuss what your options are\. They will have information about birth control, parenting, abortion, and other resources and next steps\. You can book an appointment with the [Student Health and Wellbeing](https://students.ubc.ca/health/medical-care-on-campus/) on campus, or visit a [clinic in Vancouver](https://www.optionsforsexualhealth.org/providers) to get support\.

### Preventing pregnancy 

Birth control, also known as contraception, is one way to prevent pregnancy\. There are many different methods available, and most are affordable or free in British Columbia, have little to no side\-effects, and work well when used correctly\. It’s best to talk to a healthcare provider to discuss which is best for your body and your needs\. Learn more about the [different types of birth control](https://www.sexandu.ca/contraception/)\.

You can also call [811](https://students.ubc.ca/health/health-topics/sexual-health/) in British Columbia to speak with a nurse at any time if you have questions or concerns\. It’s important to remember that no method of contraception is 100% effective, but finding the right option for you can help you feel more confident and in control of your sexual health\.

#### Accessing birth control

**

Barrier, non\-hormonal methods, such as external condoms

**

[External condoms](https://shvic.org.au/assets/resources/Condoms-external-June-2021.pdf) are a popular form of contraception and also, when used correctly, can protect against the transmission of STIs\. You can pick up free internal and external condoms at the [Wellness Centre](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-centre/), [SVPRO](https://svpro.ubc.ca/) or [AMS SASC](https://amssasc.ca/)\. They are also available for purchase in any pharmacy, sex toy store, or drugstore\.

There are also other barrier methods such as the [diaph](https://shvic.org.au/for-you/contraception/diaphragms)[r](https://shvic.org.au/for-you/contraception/diaphragms)[agm or cervical cap](https://shvic.org.au/for-you/contraception/diaphragms), which must be prescribed by a health care professional\.

**

Intrauterine Devices \(IUDs\), birth control implants, and injections

**

[Intrauterine devices \(IUDs\)](https://shvic.org.au/for-you/contraception/iud-intrauterine-device), [Contraceptive Implants,](https://shvic.org.au/for-you/contraception/contraceptive-implant-implanon) and [Contraceptive Injections](https://shvic.org.au/for-you/contraception/contraceptive-injection-depo) must be prescribed and administered by a doctor or by a nurse practitioner\.

Free, generic options are available for British Columbia residents through your [Medical Services Plan \(MSP\)](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/health/health-drug-coverage/msp/bc-residents)\. Learn more about [free contraception](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/health/health-drug-coverage/pharmacare-for-bc-residents/what-we-cover/prescription-contraceptives) for BC residents\. For non\-BC residents, there may be an associated fee\.

You can also get a prescription for an IUD or birth control implant through [Student Health and Wellbeing](https://students.ubc.ca/health/medical-care-on-campus/) on campus\. Your practitioner can discuss the device with you, as well as any possible side effects or follow\-up care and procedures\.

**

Other hormonal methods: pill, patch, ring

**

Additional hormonal methods, like the hormonal [birth control pill,](https://shvic.org.au/for-you/contraception/daily-contraceptive-pills) the [patch](https://www.optionsforsexualhealth.org/facts/birth-control/methods/skin-patch/), or a [vaginal ring](https://shvic.org.au/for-you/contraception/nuvaring-vaginal-ring), require a prescription from a healthcare provider, such as a doctor or a pharmacist\. These can be filled at most pharmacies\.

You can also book an appointment with [Stude](https://students.ubc.ca/health/student-health-service/)[n](https://students.ubc.ca/health/student-health-service/)[t Health and Wellbeing](https://students.ubc.ca/health/medical-care-on-campus/) to get a prescription or to learn more about the options\. Walk\-in clinics can also provide prescriptions\. Use the [Medimap tool](https://medimap.ca/) to find a health clinic near you\.

### Emergency contraception

If you are experiencing an unintended pregnancy, [emergency contraception](https://www.optionsforsexualhealth.org/facts/emergency-contraception/) \(EC\) may be an option for you\. 

Emergency contraception \(often known as Plan B\) is a contraceptive method used after sex has occurred\. It is used to prevent pregnancy if you had vaginal sex with no contraceptive protection or if your contraception method failed\. An example is when there is a broken condom, or when birth control pills are taken late or missed\.

Emergency contraception is available as a pill that can be taken within 5 days of vaginal sex\. The sooner you take it after the sexual encounter, the more effective it is\. Taking it within the first 12 to 24 hours after sex is the most effective\. It can be found at any pharmacy and does not require a prescription\.

Emergency Contraception is only meant to be used occasionally, and not as regular birth control\. It also does not protect against STIs\.

## Additional resources[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/sexual\-health/\#additional\-resources](https://students.ubc.ca/health/sexual-health/#additional-resources)

### Online self\-help information

[Options for Sexual Health](https://www.optionsforsexualhealth.org/)

Find clinics and resources, or contact the anonymous phone line to talk about sexual health\.

[Smart Sex Resource](https://smartsexresource.com/)

Learn about sexual health topics, STI testing options, find a clinic, or chat with a nurse online\.

### Peer support

[Wellness](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/wellness-centre/) [C](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-centre/)[entre](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/wellness-centre/)

Peer Health Educators at the Wellness Centre are trained students who can answer your sexual health questions or connect you with resources\.

[AMS Peer Support](https://www.ams.ubc.ca/student-services/peer-support/)

Get free, confidential one\-on\-one support on various topics, like relationship issues or identity questions\.

### Connect with a health professional

[Medical care on campus](https://students.ubc.ca/health/medical-care-on-campus/)

Book an appointment with a doctor or nurse for prescriptions, testing, IUD insertion, and more\.

[Mental health care at UBC](https://students.ubc.ca/health/mental-health-care-ubc/)

Student Health and Wellbeing also offers appointments with counsellors to discuss any sex, sexuality, or relationship concerns you may have\.\.

[HealthLink BC](https://www.healthlinkbc.ca/find-care/healthlink-bc-8-1-1-services)

Call the number 811 in British Columbia to speak with a nurse or get free health information and advice\.

[Sexual Violence Prevention and Response Office \(SVPRO\)](https://svpro.ubc.ca/)

Connect with an SVPRO specialist if you’ve been impacted by any form of sexual or gender\-based violence, harassment, or harm\.

[https://svpro\.ubc\.ca/](https://svpro.ubc.ca/)[AMS Sexual Assault Support Centre \(SASC\)](https://amssasc.ca/)

Get short\-term crisis support or talk to a support worker in a confidential and safe space\.

[https://svpro\.ubc\.ca/](https://svpro.ubc.ca/)[https://amssasc\.ca/](https://amssasc.ca/)[Here2Talk](https://here2talk.ca/main)

Call, chat online, or use the mobile app to get free, immediate, 24/7 mental health counselling for any concerns you may have\.

title: Sleep for success
content_markdown:
## Why sleep is important[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/wellness\-resources/sleep\-success/\#why\-sleep\-is\-important](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/sleep-success/#why-sleep-is-important)

Sleep is one of the most impactful ways to take care of your physical and mental health\.

If you’re frequently feeling tired, have trouble focusing on tasks, pull all\-nighters, or go to bed later than you want to, you may want to adjust your sleep habits\. Sleep is necessary for learning and memory retention, so getting quality sleep can help you meet your academic goals\.

### The benefits of sleeping well

A good night’s sleep has many benefits to your mental, physical, and emotional health, such as:

-   An improved ability to focus, remember, and retain new information\.
-   A stronger immune response, making it easier for your body to fight off illnesses\.
-   A greater ability to complete tasks like studying, researching, and writing\.
-   An improved mood, where you’re less likely to feel anxious, stressed, irritable, sad, or worried\.

## Strategies for better sleep[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/wellness\-resources/sleep\-success/\#strategies\-for\-better\-sleep](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/sleep-success/#strategies-for-better-sleep)

Sleep can be influenced by many things, including our environment and habits\.

As a university student, you may find it challenging to get quality sleep for many reasons, but it’s important to find out what helps and what doesn’t\. Consider what you can try to do differently throughout the day or before bedtime, to see if the changes benefit your sleep quality\.

**

Reflect on your sleep schedule

**

-   **Aim for 7 to 9 hours of sleep each night**  
    Most people need at least 7 to 9 hours of sleep each night to function optimally the next day\. Think about how many hours you need to feel rested, and remember that quality is more important than quantity\.
-   **Get up at the same time each morning**  
    On days with no morning commitments, don’t sleep in more than one hour later than your normal wake time\. This helps to keep your internal clock on schedule for sleep and wake times\.
-   **Go to sleep when you feel sleepy at night**  
    If you’re having trouble sleeping, try something relaxing that doesn’t involve screens, until you feel sleepy\. Trying to force sleep can leave you feeling frustrated, making sleep even more difficult\.

**

During the day

**

-   **Stay active**  
    Physical activity can make it easier to fall asleep\. Try a good workout after school or work, but avoid exercising close to your bedtime\.
-   **Be outdoors for part of the day**  
    Plan some outdoor time in your day, between classes, or during lunch break\. Natural daylight is helpful in maintaining your body’s sleep and wake cycles\.
-   **Be smart about napping**  
    Taking a short 20\- to 30\-minute nap can leave you feeling alert and refreshed\. Longer naps or naps too close to bedtime can affect your nighttime sleep\. Pay attention to how your naps affect your daytime alertness and nighttime sleep\.  Read more about the [benefits and concerns](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/articles/napping) of napping\.

**

Before bed

**

-   **Avoid or limit caffeine, tobacco, and alcohol before bedtime**  
    These drugs can impact your quality of sleep\. Avoiding these substances is best for your sleep, but if you must, try not to use them at least 3 hours before your bedtime\.
-   **Stop using all technology and screens at least 30 minutes before bedtime**  
    Although using a laptop, cell phone, or tablet may be necessary for studying and communicating, light from these screens block melatonin, a hormone which helps you sleep\.
-   **Unwind before bed**  
    Take time in the evening to unwind before going to bed so you’re relaxed when trying to fall asleep\. Try meditation or reading a book\.
-   **Write down your thoughts**  
    Try to note down thoughts, create a to\-do list, or jot down all the things you’re grateful for\. Keep a notepad and pen next to your bed\.

**

In your sleeping space

**

-   **Keep your bed a sleep sanctuary**  
    If your sleep and study space are in the same room, do your studying, writing, and other work at your desk, not on your bed\. Keep your bedroom quiet, dark, and well\-ventilated\.
-   **Turn off your phone**  
    Invest in an alarm clock to wake you up in the morning, and turn off your phone\. Alerts, light from your phone, and the temptation to check social media can all negatively impact your sleep\.
-   **Share your sleep habits with your roommate\(s\)**  
    Discuss your sleep habits and needs with whomever you share a space with\. Sharing preferences or expectations about noise, light, visitors, and preferred sleep and wake time can help create a more supportive sleep environment\. Learn how to [start a conversation](https://vancouver.housing.ubc.ca/residence-life/living-with-roomates/) with your roommate\.

**

During your studies

**

-   **Plan for exam season**  
    Consider how you can be at your best and take care of the basics \(e\.g\., sleep, nutrition, physical activity\) during your exams\.
-   **Avoid all\-nighters**  
    You may occasionally have to pull an all\-nighter, but not sleeping at all for even one night can affect your memory, mood, alertness, attention, and immune system\. A good night’s sleep helps you remember what you’ve been learning\. Studies have shown students who get a good night’s sleep perform better on tests than those that stay up to study more\.
-   **Learn to manage stress in your life**  
    Sometimes you can have thoughts or feelings before bed that may be stressful and interfere with your sleep\. Find out how to [reduce stress before sleep](https://www.helpguide.org/articles/stress/relaxation-techniques-for-stress-relief.htm), and remember that sleep can be a great method of self\-care\.

## When trying something new[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/wellness\-resources/sleep\-success/\#when\-trying\-something\-new](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/sleep-success/#when-trying-something-new)

When trying to improve sleep and exploring strategies, it’s important to note which strategies are working, and to be patient with yourself\.

It’s also important to remember that what works for someone else may not work for you in the same way\. Ask questions such as:

-   Am I someone who’s naturally wakeful at night, or am I an early riser? 
-   Does taking a nap or eating before bed affect my sleep? 
-   How much sleep do I need to feel rested?

To observe patterns and habits unique to you, try tracking your sleep with a [sleep diary](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/sleep-diary)\.

## Apps and interactive resources[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/wellness\-resources/sleep\-success/\#apps\-and\-interactive\-resources](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/sleep-success/#apps-and-interactive-resources)

These websites and apps have been carefully chosen by health professionals at UBC\. They’re easy and accessible tools you can use any time to improve your sleep\.

-   [Calm app](https://www.calm.com/)  
    Get more restful sleep by meditating with relaxing music with this paid app\.
-   [Headspace app student plan](https://www.headspace.com/studentplan?origin=subscriptions&origin=navigation)  
    Meditate and clear your mind for 10 minutes daily on the paid app\.
-   [Why do we sleep?](https://www.ted.com/talks/russell_foster_why_do_we_sleep)  
    Watch a TED talk video from a neuroscientist explaining the theories behind sleep\.

## Professional support[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/wellness\-resources/sleep\-success/\#professional\-support](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/sleep-success/#professional-support)

If your sleep still isn’t improving after trying these strategies, or if you’re feeling tired throughout the day despite getting plenty of sleep, talk to a health professional about your concerns\.

-   [HealthLink BC](https://www.healthlinkbc.ca/)  
    Call 811 to speak with a nurse about your concerns on sleep or learn how sleep affects your health online\.
-   [Student Health and Wellbeing](https://students.ubc.ca/health/medical-care-on-campus/)  
    Book an appointment with a doctor who can help identify what’s contributing to your sleeplessness and provide treatment\.
-   [Medimap](https://medimap.ca/clinics/walk-in-clinics/bc/vancouver)  
    Find available walk\-in clinics and wait times, and book an appointment before visiting the location\.

title: Substance use health and harm reduction
content_markdown:
Many substances, including alcohol, cannabis, nicotine \(in tobacco and some vapes\), and caffeine can alter someone’s mental, emotional, or physical state\. All substance use carries some risk, and it’s essential to consider the short\-term and long\-term effects on your wellbeing as a student\.  

No unregulated drug is safe, and prescription drugs not dispensed directly from a pharmacy also come with risks\. People should use caution with taking any unfamiliar prescription medications\.

Fentanyl and carfentanyl are strong opioid painkillers that are in the unregulated drug supply in Vancouver\. A miniscule amount of fentanyl or analogs \(carfentanyl\) can be fatal\. Fentanyl and benzodiazepines are two categories of drugs that are often found in unregulated drugs\.

You can learn more about [fentanyl](https://www.camh.ca/en/health-info/mental-illness-and-addiction-index/street-fentanyl) and about [benzodiazepines](https://www.camh.ca/en/health-info/mental-illness-and-addiction-index/anti-anxiety-medications-benzodiazepines) on the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health website\.

Other unregulated sedatives including veterinary tranquilizers like [Xylazine](https://towardtheheart.com/assets/uploads/1660762743kH775J4lVykS90oUsfpve5BeVpxIoJ9ZqpgPp3e.pdf) \(pdf\) have also been found in the unregulated drug supply\. For more information on toxic drug alerts, visit [Toward the Heart](https://towardtheheart.com/alerts), where you can also sign\-up for text message alerts\.

When using unregulated drugs, there is no way to know the exact contents of those drugs\. One form of harm reduction is [drug checking](https://students.ubc.ca/health/health-topics/substance-use-health-harm-reduction#drug-checking-testing), which can provide you with more information about the contents of those drugs\. 

Not using substances altogether has the lowest risk\. If you are using drugs, you can make a plan to reduce possible harms\. 

## Harm reduction and safer drug use[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/substance\-use\-health\-harm\-reduction/\#harm\-reduction\-and\-safer\-drug\-use](https://students.ubc.ca/health/substance-use-health-harm-reduction/#harm-reduction-and-safer-drug-use)

If you use or intend to use unregulated drugs, including prescription drugs not directly dispensed from a pharmacy, there are steps you can take to reduce potential harms: 

-   Go slow, start with a low dosage\.
-   Make a plan [for safer uses](https://towardtheheart.com/safer-use)\.
-   Have your [drugs checked](https://wellbeing.gov.bc.ca/substance-use/harm-reduction/drug-checking)\.
-   Sign up for [toxic drug and public health alerts](https://towardtheheart.com/alerts)\.  
-   Know how to recognize and respond to the signs of an overdose or toxic drug poisoning [below](https://students.ubc.ca/health/substance-use-health-harm-reduction/#recognize-the-signs-of-an-overdose-or-drug-poisoning)\.
-   Carry [naloxone](https://vancouver.housing.ubc.ca/residence-life/health-safety/safety-security/#naloxone) and other [harm reduction supplies](https://www.ams.ubc.ca/support-services/student-resources/ubc-harm-reduction-resources/)\. 
-   Do not use alone\. When possible, go to a [supervised consumption site](https://www.vch.ca/en/service/supervised-consumption-and-overdose-prevention-sites) in\-person, or use virtual supports like [NORS](https://www.nors.ca/) or [LifeGuard](https://lifeguarddh.com/)\.

Find out more by taking the [Harm Reduction 101 Canvas course](https://canvas.ubc.ca/enroll/JEAEHK)\. You can also request a workshop from [UBC Wellness Centre](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/wellness-centre/) and [AMS Peer Support](https://www.ams.ubc.ca/support-services/student-services/peer-support/)\. You can also [access the Naloxone 101 Training course](https://learninghub.phsa.ca/Courses/8458) from Toward the Heart\. 

## Fentanyl test strips[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/substance\-use\-health\-harm\-reduction/\#fentanyl\-test\-strips](https://students.ubc.ca/health/substance-use-health-harm-reduction/#fentanyl-test-strips)

Test strips can identify a small amount of fentanyl mixed in water\. You can get free, anonymous test strips at the following UBC locations: 

**AMS Nest:**  

-   AMS Resource Groups Lobby, second floor beside the Hatch Art Gallery, on the resource table upon entry 
-   AMS Peer Support, Room 3125 
-   The AMS [Sexual Assault Support Centre](https://www.amssasc.ca/find-our-office/) \(SASC\), Room 3130, on the resource table outside the Centre 

**Other locations:** 

-   [Nurse on Campus](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/nurse-campus/) nurses can demonstrate the use of test strips\.  
-   The [UBC Wellness Centre](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/wellness-centre/) resource table, room 1400 in the UBC Life Building 
-   Student Health and Wellbeing welcome desks on Level 3, in the [Gateway building](https://learningspaces.ubc.ca/buildings/gateway-health-building-gwhb/)

Use the UBC [Harm Reduction Resources List and Map](https://www.ams.ubc.ca/support-services/student-resources/ubc-harm-reduction-resources/) for a more detailed list of harm reduction resources and supplies\. 

## Drug checking \(testing\)[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/substance\-use\-health\-harm\-reduction/\#drug\-checking\-testing](https://students.ubc.ca/health/substance-use-health-harm-reduction/#drug-checking-testing)

Outside UBC, you can find [drug checking services](https://wellbeing.gov.bc.ca/substance-use/harm-reduction/drug-checking) across BC, including safer consumption sites\.

## Recognize the signs of an overdose or drug poisoning[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/substance\-use\-health\-harm\-reduction/\#recognize\-the\-signs\-of\-an\-overdose\-or\-drug\-poisoning](https://students.ubc.ca/health/substance-use-health-harm-reduction/#recognize-the-signs-of-an-overdose-or-drug-poisoning)

Look for the [following signs](https://respondtooverdose.gov.bc.ca/#recognize): 

-   Not moving and can’t be woken up, or unresponsive 
-   Breathing is slow or stopped 
-   Choking, gurgling or snoring sounds 
-   Lips and nails may be a blue or ashy colour 
-   Skin is cold and clammy 
-   Pupils are tiny\.

## Responding to an overdose or drug poisoning[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/substance\-use\-health\-harm\-reduction/\#responding\-to\-an\-overdose\-or\-drug\-poisoning](https://students.ubc.ca/health/substance-use-health-harm-reduction/#responding-to-an-overdose-or-drug-poisoning)

If someone is experiencing a known or suspected overdose, there is no time to waste\. 

1.  Immediately call [911](https://students.ubc.ca/health/health-topics/substance-use-health-harm-reduction/) 
2.  Give Naloxone 
3.  Call [Community Safety](http://communitysafety.ubc.ca/): [604 822 2222](tel:604%20822%202222) 

You are protected by the [Good Samaritan Drug Overdose Act](https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/opioids/about-good-samaritan-drug-overdose-act.html) even if you have a small amount of substance on you\. You will not get in trouble with UBC, Student Housing, the police, or Citizenship and Immigration Canada for calling 911\. 

To learn more about the Good Samaritan Act and to find out how to respond to accidental drug poisoning, enrol in the [Harm Reduction 101 Canvas course](https://canvas.ubc.ca/enroll/JEAEHK)\. 

### Naloxone kits

Naloxone is a medication that reverses overdose and accidental drug poisoning from fentanyl and other opioids\.  

You can pick up free nasal and intramuscular \(injectable\) naloxone kit to carry with you, as well as training on how to administer it, at the following locations: 

**

UBC Wellness Centre

**

Naloxone training, fentanyl test strips, drug checking mail\-in envelopes, and information on other harm reduction strategies are available for free at the [UBC Wellness Centre](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/wellness-centre/)\.

**

AMS Peer Support

**

Drop\-in free Naloxone training, free harm reduction supplies and free fentanyl test strips are available in Nest 3125 on Mon to Fri, from 11 am to 2 pm\.

**

BC pharmacies

**

Take an [online naloxone training](https://naloxonetraining.com/) and/or pick up a kit at any [BC pharmacy](https://towardtheheart.com/site-finder)\. 

Emergency nasal naloxone kits are in [UBC residences](https://vancouver.housing.ubc.ca/residence-life/health-safety/safety-security/#naloxone) and high\-traffic areas across campus\. These are often co\-located with AEDs across campus for use in an emergency\.

## When to seek help for problematic substance use[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/substance\-use\-health\-harm\-reduction/\#when\-to\-seek\-help\-for\-problematic\-substance\-use](https://students.ubc.ca/health/substance-use-health-harm-reduction/#when-to-seek-help-for-problematic-substance-use)

If you are curious about seeking help, consider the following questions, and explore support options available to UBC students below\. 

-   Are you curious to explore your relationship to substance use in a way that can positively impact your wellbeing? 
-   Do you wish to change your relationship with alcohol and/or other substances? 
-   Has your relationship with substances impacted your daily life and/or relationships? 
-   Are you looking to explore resources or reach out to someone to talk to about substance use? 

## Additional resources[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/substance\-use\-health\-harm\-reduction/\#additional\-resources](https://students.ubc.ca/health/substance-use-health-harm-reduction/#additional-resources)

The following resources are easily accessible and can help you learn more about substance use\. 

-   [HealthLink BC](https://www.healthlinkbc.ca/substance-use)  
    Call 811 at any time during the day to get information on substance use and support\.
-   [Here to Help PDF Workbook](https://www.heretohelp.bc.ca/workbook/you-and-substance-use-stuff-to-think-about-and-ways-to-make-changes)Download and print a workbook to help you reflect on your substance use\.
-   [Toward the Heart](https://towardtheheart.com/)  
    Information about opioid drug poisoning, naloxone, and other harm reduction strategies\. You can also find out where to pick up a naloxone kit across BC\.
-   [Foundry](https://foundrybc.ca/info-tools/substance-use/)  
    Find alcohol and substance use self\-check tools for youth ages 12 to 24 and learn about different types of substances\.
-   [The Junction](https://www.vch.ca/en/service/junction#overview)  
    Get community\-based support for people 19 years or older who self\-identify as maintaining or seeking recovery from substance use\.
-   [First Nations Health Authority](https://www.fnha.ca/what-we-do/mental-wellness-and-substance-use/harm-reduction-and-the-toxic-drug-crisis/indigenous-harm-reduction)  
    Explore an Indigenous\-focused All\-Paths\-Lead\-to\-Wellness approach\.
-   [Access and Assessment Centre](https://www.vch.ca/en/location-service/access-and-assessment-centre-aac-vancouver-general-hospital)Call or visit in person for emergency or non\-emergency mental health and substance use services at Vancouver General Hospital \(VGH\)\.
-   [Opioid Treatment Access Line](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/health/mental-health-and-addictions/opioid-treatment-access-line)  
    Call [1 833 804 8111](tel:18338048111) for opioid agonist treatment \(OAT\), a medication\-based option that helps prevent withdrawal symptoms and reduce overdose risks\.

## Peer support[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/substance\-use\-health\-harm\-reduction/\#peer\-support](https://students.ubc.ca/health/substance-use-health-harm-reduction/#peer-support)

It might be easier to talk with a trained peer\-support student staff about substance use\. They may understand what you’re going through and can offer helpful resources\.

The [UBC Student Recovery Community \(SRC\)](https://students.ubc.ca/health/substance-use-health-harm-reduction/ubc-student-recovery-community/) is a safe, confidential, and inclusive space for students who are in recovery or curious to explore their relationship with substances and/or non\-substance addictive behaviours such as disordered eating, pornography, gaming, gambling, and more\.

You can also visit [AMS Peer Support](https://www.ams.ubc.ca/student-services/peer-support/) for free, confidential one\-on\-one peer support, naloxone training for individuals and groups, fentanyl test strips, peer support group sessions, and workshops on mental health and harm reduction\.

### 24/7 Services

-   [Alcohol and Drug Information and Referral Service](https://www.healthlinkbc.ca/mental-health-substance-use/resources/alcohol-drug-information-referral-service)  
    Free, confidential information and referrals for any type of substance use concern\.
-   [Here2Talk](https://here2talk.ca/main)  
    Free 24/7 mental health counselling, available in multiple languages\. UBC students can reach out as often as needed, anytime, from anywhere in the world\. 
-   [988: Suicide Crisis Helpline](https://988.ca/)  
    A safe space to talk, 24 hours a day, every day of the year\. Call or text 988\.
-   [KUU\-US Crisis Line Society](https://www.kuu-uscrisisline.com/)  
    Call [1 800 588 8717](tel:18005888717), the BC Wide Indigenous Toll Free Crisis and Support Line for Indigenous individuals\.

## The intentional use of substances to facilitate sexual assault[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/substance\-use\-health\-harm\-reduction/\#the\-intentional\-use\-of\-substances\-to\-facilitate\-sexual\-assault](https://students.ubc.ca/health/substance-use-health-harm-reduction/#the-intentional-use-of-substances-to-facilitate-sexual-assault)

Using drugs, including alcohol, to deliberately create a situation in which a person is incapacitated \(and therefore cannot give consent\) to pursue sexual contact or attention is [substance\-facilitated sexual assault](https://students.ubc.ca/health/substance-use-health-harm-reduction/intentional-use-substances-facilitate-sexual-assault/)\. 

Anyone who has been impacted by substance\-facilitated sexual assault deserves support\. Confidential, non\-judgmental support is available at the [Sexual Violence Prevention and Response Office](https://svpro.ubc.ca/support/) \(SVPRO\)\. 

## UBC Wellness Centre[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/substance\-use\-health\-harm\-reduction/\#ubc\-wellness\-centre](https://students.ubc.ca/health/substance-use-health-harm-reduction/#ubc-wellness-centre)

### Pick up harm reduction supplies 

Naloxone training, fentanyl test strips, and drug checking resources are available on campus\. 

In response to the toxic drug crisis in British Columbia, naloxone kits \(both intranasal and intramuscular\), fentanyl test strips, and mail\-in drug checking kits are available for free and anonymously at the [UBC Wellness Centre](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/wellness-centre/) and [across campus](https://www.ams.ubc.ca/support-services/student-resources/ubc-harm-reduction-resources/)\.

title: Understanding stress and the stress response
content_markdown:
Stress is a normal part of the human experience\. However, everyone experiences stress differently, and stressors are unique to each person\. Below, you will find information on recognizing signs of stress, managing the stress response, and understanding different types of stressors\.

## Recognize your signs of stress[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/wellness\-resources/understanding\-stress/\#recognize\-your\-signs\-of\-stress](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/understanding-stress/#recognize-your-signs-of-stress)

The stress response can be a normal reaction to challenging or demanding situations and can be experienced in many contexts, such as school, work, and personal life\. Typically, the physical reaction to stress dissipates naturally after the immediate challenge has passed or the problem has been solved\. At other times, it lingers in ways that are not always helpful\. Increasing your awareness and understanding of this process can help you learn how to manage your stress efficiently and effectively\.

First, you need to identify when you’re experiencing stress: consider your thoughts, emotions, behaviours, and physical symptoms when faced with a challenge in life\. Maybe you feel sharp, fired up, productive, and motivated\. You rise to the challenge and tell yourself, “I can do this”\.

At other times, however, you might not feel quite so great\. Perhaps you find yourself thinking “in a loop” about how much work you have to do\. Maybe you feel overwhelmed, exhausted, or irritable\. You may also overthink, become unresponsive to others, or find it difficult to manage or focus on your tasks\. You may be experiencing sleep problems or physical symptoms, such as headaches or stomachaches\. These types of responses to stressors often act as blocks to breaking the stress cycle\. When these symptoms appear, there are strategies you can use to reduce the intensity of the stress response and move towards getting unstuck\.

## Reduce your stress response in the moment[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/wellness\-resources/understanding\-stress/\#reduce\-your\-stress\-response\-in\-the\-moment](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/understanding-stress/#reduce-your-stress-response-in-the-moment)

There are many ways to complete the stress cycle\. Below are some methods that research has shown to be effective\. You can find more in the book, [Burnout: The secret to unlocking the stress cycle](https://www.burnoutbook.net/), as well as in the Canvas course, [Mental Health: The Basics](https://canvas.ubc.ca/enroll/KFE3YB)\.

-   Physical activity
-   Breathing
-   Positive social interaction
-   Laughter
-   Affection
-   A big cry
-   Creative expression
-   Making time to unwind

### Box breathing technique

If you are experiencing a particularly stressful moment, try the [Box Breathing technique](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oN8xV3Kb5-Q)\.

The breathing exercise can help lower your heart rate, so you feel more relaxed\. You can then focus your energy on addressing the problem at hand\.

1.  Get comfortable and close your eyes\. If not, simply focus on your breathing\. Imagine your breathing following the shape of a square or box\.
2.  Inhale, preferably through your nose, for four seconds\. Hold your breath for four seconds\.
3.  Exhale slowly through your mouth for four seconds\.
4.  Pause for four seconds before breathing in again\.

Repeat this process as many times as you can\. Even thirty seconds of deep breathing may help you feel more relaxed and in control\.

## Make a plan and look for solutions[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/wellness\-resources/understanding\-stress/\#make\-a\-plan\-and\-look\-for\-solutions](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/understanding-stress/#make-a-plan-and-look-for-solutions)

Once you’ve reduced the intensity of the stress response, you can start to look for solutions to your current challenge\. Use past experiences to reflect on how you managed a similar problem, or brainstorm new ways to approach a difficult situation\.

Discuss the situation with a trusted individual, such as a friend or family member, and ask for help if you need it\. Try using the following prompts to get your problem\-solving back on track:

-   What would a good outcome in this situation look like?
-   What strengths have I drawn on so far? What is working for me?
-   How have I managed similar situations in the past? What could I learn from that?
-   What would my friend, family member, or partner suggest if they were here?
-   What would I suggest to them in a similar situation?

## Diverse experiences of stress[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/wellness\-resources/understanding\-stress/\#diverse\-experiences\-of\-stress](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/understanding-stress/#diverse-experiences-of-stress)

The stress response is something we all experience\. However, there are aspects of any individual’s identity, known as the [social determinants of health](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/health-promotion/population-health/what-determines-health.html), that can disproportionately impact health and wellbeing, including mental wellbeing and stress\.

The social determinants of health include \(but are not limited to\) income, education, childhood experiences, access to health services, gender, culture and race or racism\.

Experiences of discrimination, racism and trauma \(both historic and present\-day\) may play an essential role in health outcomes for specific groups such as Indigenous Peoples, Black People, People of Colour, LGBTQ2S\+, and people with disabilities\. These experiences shape outcomes on a number of levels: they can modify the intensity of the stress response itself, or impact an individual’s capacity to cope, and/or limit access to available supports\. 

Systemic stressors require supports that are implemented at a systems level, rather than at an individual level\.

As part of a caring and proactive community at UBC, we acknowledge these inequities and come together to support one another\. UBC is committed to addressing inequities through strategic frameworks such as the [Indigenous Strategic Plan](https://indigenous.ubc.ca/indigenous-engagement/indigenous-strategic-plan/), the [Inclusion Action Plan](https://equity.ubc.ca/about/inclusion-action-plan/inclusion-action-plan-what-we-heard/?login), and through initiatives such as the [Strategic Equity and Anti\-Racism Framework](https://antiracism.ubc.ca/)\.

As well, UBC and the broader community have resources to support students who identify as IBPOC, LGBTQ2S\+, and with disabilities, as well as [resources to support you](https://equity.ubc.ca/resources/) in being an ally to your peers with these intersecting identities\.

## Build resiliency[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/wellness\-resources/understanding\-stress/\#build\-resiliency](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/understanding-stress/#build-resiliency)

There are things you can do daily to be more resilient and feel ready to face challenges in school, work, and life\. Learn about the [24\-hour movement guidelines](https://www.participaction.com/the-science/benefits-and-guidelines/adults-18-to-64/)\.

### Take Care of the Basics

-   Get at least 7 to 9 hours of sleep each night\.
-   Fuel up on healthy foods\.
-   Stay active through exercise or any kind of joyful movement\.

### Make Time to Unwind

-   Read a book, draw, create art, journal, or write\. 
-   Connect with a friend or family member\.
-   Listen to relaxing music\.
-   Remind yourself of your strengths\.
-   Garden or visit the [UBC farmers’ market](https://ubcfarm.ubc.ca/events/category/ubc-farm-markets/)\.
-   Watch a comedy or read a funny book\.
-   Do muscle relaxation exercises\.
-   Find a quiet, safe space where you can relax, like the [UBC Nitobe Memorial Garden](https://botanicalgarden.ubc.ca/visit/nitobe-memorial-garden/)\.

### Stay connected or get involved

-   Call or spend time with friends or family when you need to talk\.
-   Build a support network by staying in touch with old friends\. 
-   Have fun and meet new people by [volunteering in your community](https://students.ubc.ca/campus-life/involved/)\.
-   Meet individuals with similar experiences and interests through an [AMS club](https://www.ams.ubc.ca/student-life/clubs/)\.

## Apps and interactive resources[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/wellness\-resources/understanding\-stress/\#apps\-and\-interactive\-resources](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/understanding-stress/#apps-and-interactive-resources)

Health professionals have carefully chosen these websites and apps at UBC\. They’re easy and accessible tools you can use at any time, to help you learn about managing stress\.

-   [MindShift app](http://www.anxietybc.com/mobile-app)   
    Learn to relax, cope with anxiety, and develop helpful ways of thinking and effective strategies for addressing anxiety\.
-   [UBC breathing videos](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLG5UGIHVtlPR6Ok0MIPzXclQPGY6hshA9)   
    Practice deep\-breathing with short videos showing beautiful scenes of nature on campus\.
-   [Headspace app student plan](https://www.headspace.com/studentplan?origin=subscriptions&origin=navigation)  
    Meditate and clear your mind for 10 minutes daily on the paid app\.
-   [HeadsUpGuys](https://headsupguys.org/)  
    Connect to a website resource aimed at helping men fight depression and prevent male suicide\.
-   [Calm app](https://www.calm.com/)  
    Get more restful sleep by meditating with relaxing music with this paid app\.
-   [Insight Timer app](https://insighttimer.com/)  
    Set a timer for yourself and practice deep\-breathing\.
-   [How to make stress your friend](https://www.ted.com/talks/kelly_mcgonigal_how_to_make_stress_your_friend?language=en)  
    Watch a TED talk video from a health psychologist to see how stress can sometimes be positive\.

## Peer support[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/wellness\-resources/understanding\-stress/\#peer\-support](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/understanding-stress/#peer-support)

It might be easier to talk with a trained student about your stress\. They may understand what you’re going through and can offer helpful resources\.

-   [AMS Peer Support](https://www.ams.ubc.ca/student-services/peer-support/)  
    Access free, confidential, one\-on\-one peer support for UBC students and staff facing a wide variety of challenges\.
-   [UBC Meditation Community](http://blogs.ubc.ca/meditation/)  
    Join UBC students and community members in free meditation sessions at the AMS Nest\.
-   [Zen at UBC](https://students.ubc.ca/campus-life/religion-spirituality/chaplains/zen-buddhist-chaplain/)Participate in meditation sittings held in the UBC Life Building twice a week\.

## Professional support[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/wellness\-resources/understanding\-stress/\#professional\-support](https://students.ubc.ca/health/wellness-resources/understanding-stress/#professional-support)

If you’ve tried resources and they aren’t helping, or if your stress or anxiety are persistent and negatively affecting your everyday life, talk to a staff member or health professional about your concerns\.

-   [UBC Student Health and Wellbeing](https://students.ubc.ca/health/mental-health-care-ubc/)  
    Book a one\-on\-one assessment for mental health concerns and get connected to resources\.
-   [Private counselling](https://students.ubc.ca/health/mental-health-care-ubc/finding-private-counsellor/)  
    Learn how to find a private mental health practitioner, such as a licensed psychologist, registered clinical counsellor, or therapist with a Master’s in Social Work\.
-   [Here2Talk](https://here2talk.ca/main)  
    Call, chat online, or use the mobile app to get free, immediate, 24/7 mental health counselling, available in various languages for post\-secondary students in British Columbia\. UBC students can reach out as often as needed, anytime, from anywhere in the world\.
-   [HealthLink BC](https://www.healthlinkbc.ca/contact-us)   
    Call 811 to speak with a nurse, or access online resources to help manage your stress\.

title: Allergy shots
content_markdown:
UBC Student Health and Wellbeing provides allergy shots, also known as antigen therapy or immunotherapy\. This is a prescribed course of injections for allergies diagnosed by an allergist\.

Allergy shots are a preventive treatment that can help your immune system build up a tolerance to something you’re allergic to\. The treatment involves injecting gradually increasing doses of the substance you’re allergic to\.

## Requesting allergy shots[https://students\.ubc\.ca/health/medical\-care\-on\-campus/allergy\-shots/\#requesting\-allergy\-shots](https://students.ubc.ca/health/medical-care-on-campus/allergy-shots/#requesting-allergy-shots)

1.  Share the [Antigen administration letter](https://students.ubc.ca/wp-content/uploads/antigen_administration_letter.pdf) \(pdf\) with your allergist and ask them to send the required information to Student Health and Wellbeing by fax at [604 484 2209](tel:604%20484%202209)\. 
2.  Call [604 822 3811](tel:604%20822%203811) your first appointment with a Student Health and Wellbeing doctor or nurse practitioner to review the documents sent by your allergist\.
3.  After seeing a Student Health and Wellbeing provider, call [604 822 3811](tel:604%20822%203811) \(extension 2\) to book your allergy shots with a Registered Nurse\. Please bring your serums with you to your appointment\. The first appointment will be 40 minutes long due to the intake procedure\.

Student Health and Wellbeing charges fees for certain tests, appointments, forms, and equipment\. If you miss or cancel your appointment without advance notice, you may also be charged a cancellation fee\. All amounts are listed in Canadian dollars and are subject to change without notice\. Please call [604 822 3811](tel:6048223811) if you have any questions about the fees\.

title: International Student Immigration FAQ
content_markdown:
> > Latest immigration updates
> 
> > Read the most up\-to\-date [immigration policy announcements](https://students.ubc.ca/news/category-ircc-policy-updates/) from IRCC covering topics like study permits, work eligibility, and more\.

The information on this page is based on information available at the time of publishing\.

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada \(IRCC\) and other government departments are constantly revising their policies\. Links for the most current information have been provided for each question; however, updates may be published elsewhere\.

-   See [IRCC’s website](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship.html) for the most up\-to\-date information\.
-   You can also review [program delivery instructions](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals.html) for officers\.

## If you are planning to travel to Canada[https://students\.ubc\.ca/international\-student\-guide/international\-immigration\-faq/\#if\-you\-are\-planning\-to\-travel\-to\-canada](https://students.ubc.ca/international-student-guide/international-immigration-faq/#if-you-are-planning-to-travel-to-canada)

If you’re an international student planning to come to UBC, there are important steps to follow before you plan your travels\.

[See the travel guide](https://students.ubc.ca/international-student-guide/travelling-to-canada/)

## Frequently Asked Questions[https://students\.ubc\.ca/international\-student\-guide/international\-immigration\-faq/\#frequently\-asked\-questions](https://students.ubc.ca/international-student-guide/international-immigration-faq/#frequently-asked-questions)

### Study permits

-   [What if I can’t travel to Canada by the start of term?](https://students.ubc.ca/international-student-guide/international-immigration-faq/#travel-to-canada-start-of-term)
-   [I received a request from IRCC to provide another document for my application\. What should I do?](https://students.ubc.ca/international-student-guide/international-immigration-faq/#ircc-request-another-document)
